title: Some moths hover at flowers so like hummingbirds that people mistake them

cover.alt: A white-lined sphinx moth with striped brown wings hovers beside a pink cluster of milkweed flowers.

body: Some hawk moths, like the white-lined sphinx in the clip, **hover in mid-air** while they sip nectar, in flight so like a hummingbird's that they are reliably mistaken for one. Hovering while feeding is known to have evolved only four times among nectar feeders. Most hawk moths also shiver their flight muscles to warm up before take-off, and in flight their bodies can pass 40 °C.

slides.alt: A white-lined sphinx moth with striped wings hovers and darts around a pink cluster of showy milkweed flowers in bright sunshine.
slides.caption: A white-lined sphinx moth hovers at showy milkweed in Seedskadee National Wildlife Refuge, moving from bloom to bloom.

slides.heading: Hawk moth tongues run from 1 cm to 28 cm long
slides.note: Hawk moths have some of the longest tongues of any insect

slides.label: the body temperature a hawk moth can pass in flight
slides.text: Before take-off, most species shiver their flight muscles to warm them up. Some can fly at more than 5.3 m/s, about 19 km/h.

slides.heading: Night flyers, mostly
slides.text: The hawk moth family has about 1,450 species. Most fly at dusk or at night, but some species fly during the day, like this one, filmed in bright sunshine.

slides.question: How do most hawk moths get ready to fly?
options: They pump air into their wings
slides.explanation: Shivering warms the flight muscles. Once airborne, a hawk moth's body can pass 40 °C.
